guard: `cotal attach` re-establishes its session when the LINK dies, and stops, saying why, when re-establishing cannot help
completionMarker: F. the two classifications the loop turns on
why: SPECIFIER BOUNDARY, and it is the reason every command here builds first. The suite reads the
code under test through TWO different paths on purpose. Cell F imports `attachRefusal` and
`isTransportEnd` from `implementations/cli/src` directly, so a mutation lands on the bytes it
grades with no build at all. Cells A to E run the real binary, `tsx bin/cotal.ts`, and
`@cotal-ai/cli` resolves to `dist/` -- so those cells audit the last BUILD. Without a build in
the command a mutation would kill the hand-built cell and leave every end-to-end cell green,
which reads as `the classifier matters` when what was actually measured is `the suite imports
the classifier`. Each mutation therefore builds the CLI first and rebuilds it in afterRestore,
because `dist/` is gitignored and git cannot be the recovery for it.
THE PAIRING IS THE POINT, not the count. Cell F builds its inputs by hand, so on its own it
proves only that the suite depends on those two functions. Mutations 1, 2 and 4 are aimed at
END-TO-END cells, which is what shows a real entry point reaches them: mutation 4 changes what
`attachRefusal` answers for `not-found` and the despawn cell goes red, having travelled the
whole path from a real `cotal stop` through the manager's reply code into the loop's verdict.
Mutation 3 is the one aimed at the hand-built cell, and it is aimed there because nothing this
harness can do makes the manager answer `permission-denied`: a static single-owner mesh mints
an admin instrument for every attach.
NOT GRADED, and MEASURED rather than asserted. The loop's own `denied` BRANCH -- the line that
turns a `denied` classification into a non-zero exit rather than another retry -- has no
end-to-end cell, for the reason above. Deleting `est.kind === \"denied\"` from that condition
is a SURVIVOR, and the first attempt to show that was thrown out: run alone it came back
UNGRADABLE, because a suite passing with a mutation applied proves nothing until something
shows the suite reaches that file at runtime at all. Applies and mutates are different
properties. Re-run PAIRED with a positive control in the same file (`not-found` -> `transient`,
which reddens cell E end to end), the control was KILLED and the branch deletion SURVIVED, so
the survivor is a real coverage gap rather than an unexecuted line. What IS proved is the
classification (mutation 3) and the loop's handling of the two classifications this harness CAN
produce, `gone` (mutation 4, cell E) and `transient` (cells A and B). The gap is the mapping
from `denied` to the exit, stated here rather than left for a reader to infer from a kill count.
The pairing is not in this config on purpose: a committed kill set with a deliberate survivor
exits non-zero for everyone who runs it afterwards, which trains readers to ignore the verdict.
MUTATION 1 IS AIMED AT `connection-closed` AND NOT AT `gap`, which is worth saying because
`gap` is the reason the original defect was FOUND. `gap` is what the client saw when the link
healed quickly; the fix stops waiting for that symptom and acts on the connection going away,
so `connection-closed` is the member of the set the end-to-end cells actually travel through.
Aiming at `gap` would have produced a survivor and a false sense of coverage.

mutations.name: `connection-closed` is dropped from the transport-class set, so the link dying is treated as the session finishing
mutations.expectRed: the link dying is announced on the terminal
mutations.cell: the link dying is announced on the terminal
mutations.note: The defect as shipped, in one list entry. Without this member the attach reads a dead link as a finished session, prints `detached from` and exits, which is the behaviour the whole change exists to remove. It is aimed at the end-to-end cell rather than at cell F deliberately: cell F would redden too, and a kill there alone would not show that the real binary travels this path.

mutations.name: `detached` joins the transport-class set, so pressing the detach key starts a reconnect instead of ending the attach
mutations.expectRed: the detach key still detaches after a reconnect
mutations.cell: the detach key still detaches after a reconnect
mutations.note: The opposite error, and the more dangerous one, because it is invisible until someone tries to leave: an operator who presses Ctrl-] gets `[cotal: connection lost, reconnecting]` and a terminal that will not give itself back. The set has to be wrong in BOTH directions to be worth asserting, so this is the pair to mutation 1.

mutations.name: a manager's `permission-denied` is classified as worth retrying
mutations.note: A manager that has said no does not change its mind, so reading its refusal as transient turns one refusal into an unbounded retry loop against it. This is the mutation aimed at the hand-built cell, and the reason is in `why`: nothing in this harness makes a static single-owner mesh answer `permission-denied`. Its sibling, mutation 4, is what shows the same function is reached from the real binary.

mutations.name: a seat the manager no longer knows is classified as worth retrying
mutations.expectRed: ...clean, saying the seat is gone (not an infinite retry against something that is not there)
mutations.cell: ...clean, saying the seat is gone (not an infinite retry against something that is not there)
mutations.note: THE REACHABILITY PROOF for the classifier. This is one line in a pure function, and the cell it reddens is a full end-to-end run: a real `cotal stop` despawns the seat while the client is reconnecting, the manager answers `not-found` on the wire, the CLI's inspect resolution carries that code, and the loop turns it into a clean exit. A kill here is the evidence that cell F is grading a function the product actually calls, rather than one the suite happens to import.
